claim: Existing in vitro models of human skeletal muscle cannot recapitulate the organization and function of native muscle.
source: Existing in vitro models of human skeletal muscle cannot recapitulate the organization and function of native muscle, limiting their use in physiological and pharmacological studies.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that sets up the motivation for the work, but no specific data or citations are provided in this sentence to support it.

claim: Bioengineered human myobundles exhibit aligned architecture.
source: These biomimetic constructs exhibit aligned architecture, multinucleated and striated myofibers, and a Pax7+ cell pool.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 1B shows aligned F-actin+ myofibers.

claim: Bioengineered human myobundles exhibit multinucleated and striated myofibers.
source: These biomimetic constructs exhibit aligned architecture, multinucleated and striated myofibers, and a Pax7+ cell pool.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 1E shows myogenin positive nuclei and Figure 1D shows striated SAA pattern.

claim: Bioengineered human myobundles contain a Pax7+ cell pool.
source: These biomimetic constructs exhibit aligned architecture, multinucleated and striated myofibers, and a Pax7+ cell pool.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 1G shows Pax7+ cells.

claim: Myobundles contract spontaneously.
source: They contract spontaneously and respond to electrical stimuli with twitch and tetanic contractions.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Video 1 shows spontaneous contractions.

claim: Myobundles respond to electrical stimuli with twitch and tetanic contractions.
source: They contract spontaneously and respond to electrical stimuli with twitch and tetanic contractions.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 2A shows twitch and tetanic force traces.

claim: Positive correlation exists between contractile force and GCaMP6-reported calcium responses in myobundles.
source: Positive correlation between contractile force and GCaMP6-reported calcium responses enables non-invasive tracking of myobundle function and drug response.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 shows the correlation plot.

claim: Myobundles maintain functional acetylcholine receptors during culture.
source: During culture, myobundles maintain functional acetylcholine receptors and structurally and functionally mature, evidenced by increased myofiber diameter and improved calcium handling and contractile strength.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 1F shows acetylcholine receptors, Figure 3E-F show functional responses to acetylcholine.

claim: Myobundles structurally and functionally mature during culture, evidenced by increased myofiber diameter.
source: During culture, myobundles maintain functional acetylcholine receptors and structurally and functionally mature, evidenced by increased myofiber diameter and improved calcium handling and contractile strength.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 1H shows increased myofiber diameter over time.

claim: Myobundles structurally and functionally mature during culture, evidenced by improved calcium handling.
source: During culture, myobundles maintain functional acetylcholine receptors and structurally and functionally mature, evidenced by increased myofiber diameter and improved calcium handling and contractile strength.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 3D shows increased calcium transient amplitude over time.

claim: Myobundles structurally and functionally mature during culture, evidenced by improved contractile strength.
source: During culture, myobundles maintain functional acetylcholine receptors and structurally and functionally mature, evidenced by increased myofiber diameter and improved calcium handling and contractile strength.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 2C shows increased twitch and tetanus forces over time.

claim: Myobundles undergo dose-dependent hypertrophy in response to diversely acting drugs similar to clinical outcomes.
source: In response to diversely acting drugs, myobundles undergo dose-dependent hypertrophy or toxic myopathy similar to clinical outcomes.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 4H-I show clenbuterol-induced hypertrophy.

claim: Myobundles undergo toxic myopathy in response to diversely acting drugs similar to clinical outcomes.
source: In response to diversely acting drugs, myobundles undergo dose-dependent hypertrophy or toxic myopathy similar to clinical outcomes.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding, and Figure 4A-F show statin and chloroquine-induced myopathy.

claim: There is a wide range of metabolic, neuromuscular, and dystrophic disorders involving skeletal muscle that are under investigation and still lacking therapies.
source: This is of particular concern as there are a wide range of metabolic, neuromuscular, and dystrophic disorders involving skeletal muscle that are under investigation and still lacking therapies.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Skeletal muscle is central to diseases with high societal impact including diabetes and obesity.
source: Skeletal muscle is also central to diseases with high societal impact and those that do not have adequate animal models, including diabetes, obesity, and different dystrophies.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of skeletal muscle in disease, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Skeletal muscle secretes contraction-dependent myokines.
source: Furthermore, through secretion of contraction-dependent myokines, skeletal muscle has been strongly implicated in organ–organ interactions including processes as diverse as cognition, inflammation, cancer, and aging (Pedersen and Febbraio, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pedersen and Febbraio, 2012.

claim: Skeletal muscle has been strongly implicated in organ-organ interactions including cognition, inflammation, cancer, and aging.
source: Furthermore, through secretion of contraction-dependent myokines, skeletal muscle has been strongly implicated in organ–organ interactions including processes as diverse as cognition, inflammation, cancer, and aging (Pedersen and Febbraio, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Pedersen and Febbraio, 2012.

claim: Cerivastatin was well tolerated in mice but caused fatal rhabdomyolysis in humans.
source: The need for an accurate preclinical model of human skeletal muscle was exemplified by the market withdrawal of cerivastatin that was well tolerated in mice but caused fatal rhabdomyolysis in humans (von Keutz and Schluter, 1998; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to von Keutz and Schluter, 1998 and Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: Cerivastatin was withdrawn from the market.
source: The need for an accurate preclinical model of human skeletal muscle was exemplified by the market withdrawal of cerivastatin that was well tolerated in mice but caused fatal rhabdomyolysis in humans (von Keutz and Schluter, 1998; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to von Keutz and Schluter, 1998 and Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: Expansion of primary human myoblasts and formation of myotubes in 2D systems is well known.
source: Expansion of primary human myoblasts and formation of myotubes in two-dimensional (2D) systems is well known, however, these cultures are difficult to maintain over long times, lack the architecture of native muscle, and require complex media components to initiate spontaneous contractions (Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014.

claim: 2D cultures of human myoblasts are difficult to maintain over long times.
source: Expansion of primary human myoblasts and formation of myotubes in two-dimensional (2D) systems is well known, however, these cultures are difficult to maintain over long times, lack the architecture of native muscle, and require complex media components to initiate spontaneous contractions (Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014.

claim: 2D cultures of human myoblasts lack the architecture of native muscle.
source: Expansion of primary human myoblasts and formation of myotubes in two-dimensional (2D) systems is well known, however, these cultures are difficult to maintain over long times, lack the architecture of native muscle, and require complex media components to initiate spontaneous contractions (Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014.

claim: 2D cultures of human myoblasts require complex media components to initiate spontaneous contractions.
source: Expansion of primary human myoblasts and formation of myotubes in two-dimensional (2D) systems is well known, however, these cultures are difficult to maintain over long times, lack the architecture of native muscle, and require complex media components to initiate spontaneous contractions (Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Blau and Webster, 1981; Eberli et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2014.

claim: The contractile force of single, in vitro cultured human myofibers can be measured.
source: The contractile force of single, in vitro cultured human myofibers can be measured (Smith et al., 2014), though such a system is limited by its inability to investigate biochemical changes or cell–matrix interactions that can be critical in different pathologies including muscle dystrophies and wasting disorders (Ciciliot et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2014.

claim: Single myofiber systems are limited by their inability to investigate biochemical changes or cell-matrix interactions.
source: The contractile force of single, in vitro cultured human myofibers can be measured (Smith et al., 2014), though such a system is limited by its inability to investigate biochemical changes or cell–matrix interactions that can be critical in different pathologies including muscle dystrophies and wasting disorders (Ciciliot et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ciciliot et al., 2013.

claim: Cell-matrix interactions can be critical in muscle dystrophies and wasting disorders.
source: The contractile force of single, in vitro cultured human myofibers can be measured (Smith et al., 2014), though such a system is limited by its inability to investigate biochemical changes or cell–matrix interactions that can be critical in different pathologies including muscle dystrophies and wasting disorders (Ciciliot et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ciciliot et al., 2013.

claim: 3D culture models of rodent skeletal muscle have measureable contractile force.
source: While three-dimensional (3D) culture models of rodent skeletal muscle have measureable contractile force (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000; Huang et al., 2005; Hinds et al., 2011; Juhas et al., 2014; Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and can be applied to drug testing (Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and disease modeling (Lee and Vandenburgh, 2013), in vitro 3D systems using primary human myoblasts rely on measurements of passive force (Powell et al., 2002; Moon du et al., 2008; Mudera et al., 2010) which is not specific to functional skeletal muscle.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dennis and Kosnik, 2000; Huang et al., 2005; Hinds et al., 2011; Juhas et al., 2014; Vandenburgh et al., 2008.

claim: 3D culture models of rodent skeletal muscle can be applied to drug testing.
source: While three-dimensional (3D) culture models of rodent skeletal muscle have measureable contractile force (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000; Huang et al., 2005; Hinds et al., 2011; Juhas et al., 2014; Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and can be applied to drug testing (Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and disease modeling (Lee and Vandenburgh, 2013), in vitro 3D systems using primary human myoblasts rely on measurements of passive force (Powell et al., 2002; Moon du et al., 2008; Mudera et al., 2010) which is not specific to functional skeletal muscle.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vandenburgh et al., 2008.

claim: 3D culture models of rodent skeletal muscle can be applied to disease modeling.
source: While three-dimensional (3D) culture models of rodent skeletal muscle have measureable contractile force (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000; Huang et al., 2005; Hinds et al., 2011; Juhas et al., 2014; Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and can be applied to drug testing (Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and disease modeling (Lee and Vandenburgh, 2013), in vitro 3D systems using primary human myoblasts rely on measurements of passive force (Powell et al., 2002; Moon du et al., 2008; Mudera et al., 2010) which is not specific to functional skeletal muscle.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lee and Vandenburgh, 2013.

claim: In vitro 3D systems using primary human myoblasts rely on measurements of passive force.
source: While three-dimensional (3D) culture models of rodent skeletal muscle have measureable contractile force (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000; Huang et al., 2005; Hinds et al., 2011; Juhas et al., 2014; Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and can be applied to drug testing (Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and disease modeling (Lee and Vandenburgh, 2013), in vitro 3D systems using primary human myoblasts rely on measurements of passive force (Powell et al., 2002; Moon du et al., 2008; Mudera et al., 2010) which is not specific to functional skeletal muscle.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Powell et al., 2002; Moon du et al., 2008; Mudera et al., 2010.

claim: Passive force measurements are not specific to functional skeletal muscle.
source: While three-dimensional (3D) culture models of rodent skeletal muscle have measureable contractile force (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000; Huang et al., 2005; Hinds et al., 2011; Juhas et al., 2014; Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and can be applied to drug testing (Vandenburgh et al., 2008) and disease modeling (Lee and Vandenburgh, 2013), in vitro 3D systems using primary human myoblasts rely on measurements of passive force (Powell et al., 2002; Moon du et al., 2008; Mudera et al., 2010) which is not specific to functional skeletal muscle.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing systems, drawing on knowledge of muscle physiology.

claim: Myobundles contain densely packed and aligned myofibers embedded in a laminin-rich matrix after 2-week culture.
source: After 2-week culture, the myobundles contained densely packed and aligned myofibers embedded in a laminin-rich matrix (Figure 1B) and surrounded at the periphery by vimentin+ fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing F-actin and laminin staining.

claim: Myobundles are surrounded at the periphery by vimentin+ fibroblasts.
source: After 2-week culture, the myobundles contained densely packed and aligned myofibers embedded in a laminin-rich matrix (Figure 1B) and surrounded at the periphery by vimentin+ fibroblasts (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C showing vimentin staining.

claim: Mature structure of myofibers is evident by the expression of myosin heavy chain.
source: Mature structure of the myofibers was evident by the expression of myosin heavy chain (MYH), sarcomeric alpha-actinin (SAA) cross-striations, and multiple myogenin+ nuclei (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing MYH expression.

claim: Mature structure of myofibers is evident by sarcomeric alpha-actinin cross-striations.
source: Mature structure of the myofibers was evident by the expression of myosin heavy chain (MYH), sarcomeric alpha-actinin (SAA) cross-striations, and multiple myogenin+ nuclei (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1D showing SAA cross-striations.

claim: Mature structure of myofibers is evident by multiple myogenin+ nuclei.
source: Mature structure of the myofibers was evident by the expression of myosin heavy chain (MYH), sarcomeric alpha-actinin (SAA) cross-striations, and multiple myogenin+ nuclei (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1E showing myogenin+ nuclei.

claim: Acetylcholine receptors are necessary for neuromuscular junction formation.
source: Of functional importance, acetylcholine receptors, which are necessary for neuromuscular junction formation, were present at the myofiber surface (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of acetylcholine receptors, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: Acetylcholine receptors are present at the myofiber surface in myobundles.
source: Of functional importance, acetylcholine receptors, which are necessary for neuromuscular junction formation, were present at the myofiber surface (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1F showing bungarotoxin-labeled acetylcholine receptors.

claim: A fraction of cells in myobundles continue to express the satellite cell marker Pax7.
source: While the majority of expanded myogenic cells fused to form myofibers, a fraction of cells continued to express the satellite cell marker Pax7 (Figure 1G), suggesting regenerative capacity as described in a rat culture model (Juhas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1G showing Pax7+ cells.

claim: Pax7+ cells in myobundles suggest regenerative capacity.
source: While the majority of expanded myogenic cells fused to form myofibers, a fraction of cells continued to express the satellite cell marker Pax7 (Figure 1G), suggesting regenerative capacity as described in a rat culture model (Juhas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of Pax7+ cells and comparison to a rat model cited as Juhas et al., 2014.

claim: Myofiber diameter increases progressively with time in culture from 13.5 ± 1.5 µm at 1 week to 21.8 ± 2.8 µm at 4 weeks.
source: With time in culture, structural maturation of myobundles was evident from the progressive increase in myofiber diameter (13.5 ± 1.5 µm and 21.8 ± 2.8 µm at 1 and 4 weeks of culture, Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and expression of the muscle-specific proteins (MYH, SAA, and muscle creatine kinase (MCK), Figure 1I), while myofiber length and myonuclei number (524 ± 70 and 7 ± 3.6, respectively, at 3 weeks of differentiation) remained relatively steady with time of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 1H.

claim: Expression of muscle-specific proteins MYH, SAA, and MCK increases with time in culture.
source: With time in culture, structural maturation of myobundles was evident from the progressive increase in myofiber diameter (13.5 ± 1.5 µm and 21.8 ± 2.8 µm at 1 and 4 weeks of culture, Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and expression of the muscle-specific proteins (MYH, SAA, and muscle creatine kinase (MCK), Figure 1I), while myofiber length and myonuclei number (524 ± 70 and 7 ± 3.6, respectively, at 3 weeks of differentiation) remained relatively steady with time of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1I showing western blot data.

claim: Myofiber length remains relatively steady with time of culture at 524 ± 70 µm at 3 weeks of differentiation.
source: With time in culture, structural maturation of myobundles was evident from the progressive increase in myofiber diameter (13.5 ± 1.5 µm and 21.8 ± 2.8 µm at 1 and 4 weeks of culture, Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and expression of the muscle-specific proteins (MYH, SAA, and muscle creatine kinase (MCK), Figure 1I), while myofiber length and myonuclei number (524 ± 70 and 7 ± 3.6, respectively, at 3 weeks of differentiation) remained relatively steady with time of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Myonuclei number remains relatively steady with time of culture at 7 ± 3.6 at 3 weeks of differentiation.
source: With time in culture, structural maturation of myobundles was evident from the progressive increase in myofiber diameter (13.5 ± 1.5 µm and 21.8 ± 2.8 µm at 1 and 4 weeks of culture, Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) and expression of the muscle-specific proteins (MYH, SAA, and muscle creatine kinase (MCK), Figure 1I), while myofiber length and myonuclei number (524 ± 70 and 7 ± 3.6, respectively, at 3 weeks of differentiation) remained relatively steady with time of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The amplitude of induced contractile force by electrical or chemical stimulation is a key parameter used to evaluate skeletal muscle function both in vivo and ex vivo on isolated muscle fibers.
source: The amplitude of induced contractile force by electrical or chemical stimulation is a key parameter used to evaluate skeletal muscle function both in vivo and ex vivo on isolated muscle fibers (Fuglevand et al., 1999; Bottinelli and Reggiani, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fuglevand et al., 1999 and Bottinelli and Reggiani, 2000.

claim: bFGF has been shown to improve expansion of myogenic cells.
source: A second growth media containing 5 ng/ml bFGF and 20% fetal calf serum was used during optimization as it was previously shown to improve expansion of myogenic cells (Ham et al., 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ham et al., 1988.

claim: Myobundles made of EGF-expanded cells had superior contractile function compared to bFGF-expanded cells.
source: Despite comparable myoblast purity and myofiber formation in 2D culture, myobundles made of EGF-expanded cells had superior contractile function (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing contractile force comparison.

claim: Myobundles exhibit stronger contraction with an increase in stimulation frequency.
source: In addition to spontaneous contractions, myobundles also contracted in response to electrical stimulation (Video 2) and, similar to native muscle (Rassier et al., 1999), exhibited stronger contraction with an increase in stimulation frequency and myobundle length (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myobundles exhibit stronger contraction with an increase in myobundle length.
source: In addition to spontaneous contractions, myobundles also contracted in response to electrical stimulation (Video 2) and, similar to native muscle (Rassier et al., 1999), exhibited stronger contraction with an increase in stimulation frequency and myobundle length (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Native muscle exhibits stronger contraction with an increase in stimulation frequency and length.
source: In addition to spontaneous contractions, myobundles also contracted in response to electrical stimulation (Video 2) and, similar to native muscle (Rassier et al., 1999), exhibited stronger contraction with an increase in stimulation frequency and myobundle length (Figure 2A–B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rassier et al., 1999.

claim: Amplitudes of twitch and tetanus force in myobundles increased over 4 weeks in culture.
source: In concert with observed structural maturation, amplitudes of twitch and tetanus force in myobundles increased over 4 weeks in culture (Figure 2C), while twitch kinetics remained unchanged (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Twitch kinetics in myobundles remained unchanged over 4 weeks in culture.
source: In concert with observed structural maturation, amplitudes of twitch and tetanus force in myobundles increased over 4 weeks in culture (Figure 2C), while twitch kinetics remained unchanged (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Myobundles from ten different cell sources contracted in response to electrical stimulation with an average specific force of 2.1 ± 0.9 mN/mm2 for twitch.
source: Expanded cells from all ten sources formed functional myobundles that contracted in response to electrical stimulation with an average specific force of 2.1 ± 0.9 mN/mm2 and 7.0 ± 2.2 mN/mm2 for twitch and tetanus, respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Myobundles from ten different cell sources contracted in response to electrical stimulation with an average specific force of 7.0 ± 2.2 mN/mm2 for tetanus.
source: Expanded cells from all ten sources formed functional myobundles that contracted in response to electrical stimulation with an average specific force of 2.1 ± 0.9 mN/mm2 and 7.0 ± 2.2 mN/mm2 for twitch and tetanus, respectively (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: The average tetanus force of myobundles is similar to values measured in fetal human muscle.
source: The average tetanus force was similar to values measured in fetal human muscle (Racca et al., 2013) and an order of magnitude lower than values reported for adult muscle (Racca et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2014), while average tetanus-to-twitch ratio (3.5 ± 0.8, Figure 2E) was within the normal adult range (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to published data, supported by a citation to Racca et al., 2013.

claim: The average tetanus force of myobundles is an order of magnitude lower than values reported for adult muscle.
source: The average tetanus force was similar to values measured in fetal human muscle (Racca et al., 2013) and an order of magnitude lower than values reported for adult muscle (Racca et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2014), while average tetanus-to-twitch ratio (3.5 ± 0.8, Figure 2E) was within the normal adult range (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to published data, supported by citations to Racca et al., 2013 and Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: The average tetanus-to-twitch ratio of myobundles is 3.5 ± 0.8.
source: The average tetanus force was similar to values measured in fetal human muscle (Racca et al., 2013) and an order of magnitude lower than values reported for adult muscle (Racca et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2014), while average tetanus-to-twitch ratio (3.5 ± 0.8, Figure 2E) was within the normal adult range (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 2E.

claim: The average tetanus-to-twitch ratio of myobundles is within the normal adult range.
source: The average tetanus force was similar to values measured in fetal human muscle (Racca et al., 2013) and an order of magnitude lower than values reported for adult muscle (Racca et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2014), while average tetanus-to-twitch ratio (3.5 ± 0.8, Figure 2E) was within the normal adult range (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to published data, supported by a citation to Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: The kinetic parameters of twitch contraction in myobundles were on average twofold slower than those of adult human muscle.
source: The kinetic parameters of twitch contraction were also evaluated for each donor sample (Figure 2F) and were on average twofold slower than those of adult human muscle (Fuglevand et al., 1999) and comparable to those of single in vitro cultured human myotubes (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to published data, supported by a citation to Fuglevand et al., 1999.

claim: The kinetic parameters of twitch contraction in myobundles were comparable to those of single in vitro cultured human myotubes.
source: The kinetic parameters of twitch contraction were also evaluated for each donor sample (Figure 2F) and were on average twofold slower than those of adult human muscle (Fuglevand et al., 1999) and comparable to those of single in vitro cultured human myotubes (Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison to published data, supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2014.

claim: Calcium handling is critical to normal muscle function.
source: To expand the utility of the myobundle platform, we incorporated a capability for non-invasive real-time monitoring of calcium transients in myobundles as calcium handling is critical to normal muscle function and can be affected by pathological conditions including dystrophic disorders and malignant hyperthermia (Berchtold et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berchtold et al., 2000.

claim: Calcium handling can be affected by pathological conditions including dystrophic disorders and malignant hyperthermia.
source: To expand the utility of the myobundle platform, we incorporated a capability for non-invasive real-time monitoring of calcium transients in myobundles as calcium handling is critical to normal muscle function and can be affected by pathological conditions including dystrophic disorders and malignant hyperthermia (Berchtold et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Berchtold et al., 2000.

claim: The amplitude of calcium transients in myobundles increased in response to 10 Hz (tetanic) vs single (twitch) stimuli.
source: In response to 10 Hz (tetanic) vs single (twitch) stimuli, the amplitude of calcium transients increased (Figure 3C–D), as measured by normalized change in fluorescence intensity (ΔF/F), similar to the increase in contractile force with tetanic stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3C-D.

claim: Calcium transient amplitude increased with longer time in culture.
source: Additionally, with longer time in culture, calcium transient amplitude increased (Figure 3D) and correlated with the contractile force amplitude measured in the same bundles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Calcium transient amplitude correlated with contractile force amplitude in myobundles.
source: Additionally, with longer time in culture, calcium transient amplitude increased (Figure 3D) and correlated with the contractile force amplitude measured in the same bundles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing the correlation.

claim: Caffeine generates concentration-dependent calcium release and contraction in skeletal muscle by opening of ryanodine receptors.
source: By opening of ryanodine receptors, caffeine is known to generate concentration-dependent calcium release and contraction in skeletal muscle (Moulds and Denborough, 1974; Berchtold et al., 2000), as was observed in myobundles from different donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 4).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Moulds and Denborough, 1974 and Berchtold et al., 2000.

claim: Caffeine generates concentration-dependent calcium release in myobundles from different donors.
source: By opening of ryanodine receptors, caffeine is known to generate concentration-dependent calcium release and contraction in skeletal muscle (Moulds and Denborough, 1974; Berchtold et al., 2000), as was observed in myobundles from different donors (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Video 4.

claim: ACh is released at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate muscle contraction via opening of ligand-gated Na/K-permeable channels and voltage-gated Ca channels.
source: ACh is released at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate muscle contraction via opening of ligand-gated Na/K-permeable channels and voltage-gated Ca channels, while ACh receptors are a target of different muscle relaxants and toxins (Kalamida et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kalamida et al., 2007.

claim: ACh receptors are a target of different muscle relaxants and toxins.
source: ACh is released at the neuromuscular junction to stimulate muscle contraction via opening of ligand-gated Na/K-permeable channels and voltage-gated Ca channels, while ACh receptors are a target of different muscle relaxants and toxins (Kalamida et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kalamida et al., 2007.

claim: The degree of calcium release in response to a bolus of 10 mM ACh was comparable to that from electrically stimulated tetanus.
source: The degree of calcium release in response to a bolus of 10 mM ACh (Figure 3E, Video 5) was comparable to that from electrically stimulated tetanus (Figure 3F) and unchanged throughout the entire culture period (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3E-F.

claim: Calcium release in response to ACh was unchanged throughout the entire culture period.
source: The degree of calcium release in response to a bolus of 10 mM ACh (Figure 3E, Video 5) was comparable to that from electrically stimulated tetanus (Figure 3F) and unchanged throughout the entire culture period (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Tubocurarine blocked ACh-induced calcium transients but not electrically-induced calcium transients.
source: Tubocurarine, a muscle relaxant, blocked ACh (but not electrically) induced calcium transients (Figure 3F) and contractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C), mimicking the neuromuscular block observed in vivo (Secher et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-C.

claim: Tubocurarine blocked ACh-induced contractions but not electrically-induced contractions.
source: Tubocurarine, a muscle relaxant, blocked ACh (but not electrically) induced calcium transients (Figure 3F) and contractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C), mimicking the neuromuscular block observed in vivo (Secher et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 3B-C.

claim: Tubocurarine mimics the neuromuscular block observed in vivo.
source: Tubocurarine, a muscle relaxant, blocked ACh (but not electrically) induced calcium transients (Figure 3F) and contractions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B–C), mimicking the neuromuscular block observed in vivo (Secher et al., 1982).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Secher et al., 1982.

claim: Statins are widely prescribed to prevent coronary artery disease.
source: Statins are widely prescribed to prevent coronary artery disease, however even at normal doses some of them can induce significant myopathic weakness and rhabdomyolysis after as early as 2 weeks of use (Dobkin, 2005; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about clinical use of statins, drawing on established knowledge and supported by citations.

claim: Even at normal doses some statins can induce significant myopathic weakness and rhabdomyolysis after as early as 2 weeks of use.
source: Statins are widely prescribed to prevent coronary artery disease, however even at normal doses some of them can induce significant myopathic weakness and rhabdomyolysis after as early as 2 weeks of use (Dobkin, 2005; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dobkin, 2005 and Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: Lovastatin has 100-fold lower bioavailability and bioactivity compared to cerivastatin.
source: We tested the effects of lovastatin and cerivastatin at their clinically-relevant dose ranges (100-fold higher for lovastatin due its lower bioavailability and bioactivity [Kantola et al., 1998; Shitara and Sugiyama, 2006]) encompassing both maximum therapeutic blood serum concentrations and higher doses known to accelerate myopathic induction (Dobkin, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kantola et al., 1998 and Shitara and Sugiyama, 2006.

claim: 2-week application of each statin was well tolerated in myobundles derived from two of three donors at their respective therapeutic doses.
source: In our studies, 2-week application of each statin was well tolerated in the myobundles derived from two of three donors at their respective therapeutic doses, while higher doses induced significant contractile weakness in the myobundles from all donors (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A-B.

claim: Higher doses of statins induced significant contractile weakness in myobundles from all donors.
source: In our studies, 2-week application of each statin was well tolerated in the myobundles derived from two of three donors at their respective therapeutic doses, while higher doses induced significant contractile weakness in the myobundles from all donors (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A-B.

claim: Murine engineered muscle tissues exhibited a sharp decrease in contractile function even at the lowest statin dose tested.
source: Unlike human myobundles that replicated clinical response, murine engineered muscle tissues in previous studies exhibited a sharp decrease in contractile function even at the lowest statin dose tested (Vandenburgh et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Vandenburgh et al., 2008.

claim: Human myobundles recapitulated the histopathology of statin-associated myopathy characterized by dose-dependent lipid accumulation.
source: Human myobundles also recapitulated the histopathology of statin-associated myopathy characterized by dose-dependent lipid accumulation (Thompson et al., 2006) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4C showing Oil Red O staining.

claim: 1-week exposure of myobundles to chloroquine resulted in dose-dependent decrease of contractile force.
source: With increasing doses of chloroquine, myobundles from all donors exhibited a decrease in contractile force generation (Figure 4D), which was associated with the autophagic buildup marked by conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II and a decrease in the expression of the contractile protein SAA (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: Chloroquine-induced decrease in contractile force was associated with autophagic buildup marked by conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II.
source: With increasing doses of chloroquine, myobundles from all donors exhibited a decrease in contractile force generation (Figure 4D), which was associated with the autophagic buildup marked by conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II and a decrease in the expression of the contractile protein SAA (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E-F.

claim: Chloroquine-induced decrease in contractile force was associated with a decrease in the expression of the contractile protein SAA.
source: With increasing doses of chloroquine, myobundles from all donors exhibited a decrease in contractile force generation (Figure 4D), which was associated with the autophagic buildup marked by conversion of LC3B-I to LC3B-II and a decrease in the expression of the contractile protein SAA (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4E-F.

claim: The outcomes of chloroquine treatment in myobundles were consistent with autophagic-related myopathy seen in humans treated with chloroquine.
source: These outcomes were consistent with autophagic-related myopathy seen in humans treated with chloroquine (Shintani and Klionsky, 2004; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Shintani and Klionsky, 2004 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: Clenbuterol is a β2-adrenergic agonist with both short and long-term concentration-dependent effects on muscle.
source: Clenbuterol is a β2-adrenergic agonist with both short and long-term concentration-dependent effects on muscle, improving contractile force and hypertrophy at low concentrations, while inducing apoptosis and necrosis at high concentrations (Burniston et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Burniston et al., 2006.

claim: Clenbuterol improves contractile force and hypertrophy at low concentrations.

claim: Clenbuterol induces apoptosis and necrosis at high concentrations.

claim: Clenbuterol and other β-agonists are under investigation for prevention of muscle wasting.
source: Clenbuterol and other β-agonists are under investigation for prevention of muscle wasting (Ryall and Lynch, 2008), however, species-dependent differences in their anabolic effects limit the usefulness of preclinical animal studies (Chen and Alway, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ryall and Lynch, 2008.

claim: Species-dependent differences in the anabolic effects of β-agonists limit the usefulness of preclinical animal studies.
source: Clenbuterol and other β-agonists are under investigation for prevention of muscle wasting (Ryall and Lynch, 2008), however, species-dependent differences in their anabolic effects limit the usefulness of preclinical animal studies (Chen and Alway, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chen and Alway, 2000.

claim: Both acute and chronic application of clenbuterol induced an in vivo-like biphasic dose-dependent effect on contractile force generation of myobundles.
source: In our studies, both acute and chronic application of clenbuterol induced an in vivo-like biphasic dose-dependent effect on contractile force generation of myobundles (Figure 4G–H) with the typical anabolic response and stronger contractions at 0.1 µM and diminished contractile response above 1 μM.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4G-H.

claim: Clenbuterol at 0.1 µM induced stronger contractions in myobundles.
source: In our studies, both acute and chronic application of clenbuterol induced an in vivo-like biphasic dose-dependent effect on contractile force generation of myobundles (Figure 4G–H) with the typical anabolic response and stronger contractions at 0.1 µM and diminished contractile response above 1 μM.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4G-H.

claim: Clenbuterol above 1 μM induced diminished contractile response in myobundles.
source: In our studies, both acute and chronic application of clenbuterol induced an in vivo-like biphasic dose-dependent effect on contractile force generation of myobundles (Figure 4G–H) with the typical anabolic response and stronger contractions at 0.1 µM and diminished contractile response above 1 μM.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4G-H.

claim: The positive inotropic effect of 0.1 µM clenbuterol was partially attributed to myofiber hypertrophy.
source: The observed positive inotropic effect of 0.1 µM clenbuterol was partially attributed to myofiber hypertrophy (Figure 4I) and was confirmed in myobundles from multiple donors, resulting in an average force increase of 43.2 ± 10.8% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: 0.1 µM clenbuterol resulted in an average force increase of 43.2 ± 10.8% in myobundles from multiple donors.
source: The observed positive inotropic effect of 0.1 µM clenbuterol was partially attributed to myofiber hypertrophy (Figure 4I) and was confirmed in myobundles from multiple donors, resulting in an average force increase of 43.2 ± 10.8% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text with specific measurements and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Myobundles recapitulate key functional aspects of human skeletal muscle including a functioning contractile apparatus.
source: Myobundles recapitulate key functional aspects of human skeletal muscle including a functioning contractile apparatus, responsive acetylcholine and β2-adrenergic receptors, and physiological calcium handling, all of which are involved in pharmacological side effects in humans (Bowes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data presented throughout the paper.

claim: A relatively high cell density contributed to the robust formation of functional human engineered muscle.

claim: Binding affinity to β2-adrenergic receptors is one of the standard tests for drug specificity.
source: Currently, binding affinity to β2-adrenergic receptors is one of the standard tests for drug specificity (Bowes et al., 2012) and is also a potential target for therapies in muscle wasting disorders (Ryall and Lynch, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Bowes et al., 2012.

source: Overall, these results suggest that myobundles closely mimic the functional responses of native human muscle through multiple signaling pathways and could provide a pre-clinical assay for predictive screening of novel therapeutics for a broad range of muscle-related disorders.

claim: Myogenic cells were encapsulated at 15 × 10^6 cells/ml (7.5 × 10^5 cells per myobundle).
source: Expanded myogenic cells were dissociated in 0.025% trypsin-EDTA to a single cell suspension and encapsulated in a fibrinogen (Akron, Boca Raton, FL) and matrigel solution on laser cut Cerex frames (9.2 × 9.5 mm outer dimensions, 6.8 × 8.3 mm inner dimensions) within PDMS molds (cast from Teflon masters and pretreated with pluronic) at 15 × 106 cells/ml (7.5 × 105 cells per myobundle).
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used, describing the cell density.

claim: Starting from a 50 mg donor biopsy, typical cell expansion for 5 passages can allow generation of at least 1000 myobundles with a total mass of >5 g.
source: Starting from a 50 mg donor biopsy, typical cell expansion for 5 passages can allow generation of at least 1000 myobundles with a total mass of >5 g, representing a >100-fold amplification of muscle mass when going from native to engineered tissue system.
evidence: This is a statement about the scalability of the system, based on experimental observations.

claim: The myobundle system represents a >100-fold amplification of muscle mass when going from native to engineered tissue.
source: Starting from a 50 mg donor biopsy, typical cell expansion for 5 passages can allow generation of at least 1000 myobundles with a total mass of >5 g, representing a >100-fold amplification of muscle mass when going from native to engineered tissue system.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data about cell expansion and myobundle generation.

claim: Myobundles began to spontaneously twitch after 3-5 days of differentiation.
source: Following hydrogel compaction for 3–5 days, low serum media was applied to induce myofiber formation and differentiation. After an additional 3–5 days, the myobundles began to spontaneously twitch (Video 1), which was previously reported only in rodent 3D muscle constructs (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Video 1.

claim: Spontaneous twitching in 3D muscle constructs was previously reported only in rodent systems.
source: Following hydrogel compaction for 3–5 days, low serum media was applied to induce myofiber formation and differentiation. After an additional 3–5 days, the myobundles began to spontaneously twitch (Video 1), which was previously reported only in rodent 3D muscle constructs (Dennis and Kosnik, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dennis and Kosnik, 2000.

claim: Human myobundles showed higher sensitivity to cerivastatin than lovastatin.
source: Similar to clinical reports, human myobundles showed higher sensitivity to cerivastatin than lovastatin (Shitara and Sugiyama, 2006) and at excessive statin concentrations displayed progressive weakness and lipid accumulation, suggestive of equivalent mechanisms of action in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 4A-B, with a citation to Shitara and Sugiyama, 2006.

claim: At excessive statin concentrations, myobundles displayed progressive weakness and lipid accumulation, suggestive of equivalent mechanisms of action in vitro and in vivo.

evidence: This is stated as a capability of the system, with citations to Dobkin, 2005 and Thompson et al., 2006.
